content: Women aged 15 to 24 years experience high rates of unintended pregnancies, with over half of them expressing a desire to avoid pregnancy. However, this age group also demonstrates higher rates of contraceptive failure within the first year of use compared to older women. Additionally, discontinuation of contraceptive methods is a significant issue among young women. Concerns about the acceptability and effectiveness of hormonal or intrauterine contraceptives in adolescents and young women may discourage healthcare providers from recommending these methods. The objective of this study was to compare the rates of contraceptive failure (pregnancy) and to evaluate the continuation rates of hormonal and intrauterine contraceptive methods in women aged 25 years and younger. A systematic search was conducted up to August 4, 2015, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared hormonal or intrauterine contraceptive methods in this population. Databases searched included the Cochrane Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, POPLINE, CINAHL, and LILACS. Ongoing trials were also identified through ClinicalTrials.gov and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). The inclusion criteria for the study were RCTs in any language that reported contraceptive failure rates for hormonal or intrauterine methods compared to another contraceptive method in women aged 25 years and younger. Comparators could include another intrauterine contraceptive, a different hormonal contraceptive, a different dose of the same method, or a non-hormonal contraceptive. The treatment duration had to be at least three months, and the primary outcome of interest was the contraceptive failure rate (pregnancy). The secondary outcome was the continuation rate of the contraceptive method. Data extraction was performed by one author and verified by another. For dichotomous outcomes, the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio (OR) with a 95% confidence interval (CI) was calculated. Due to variability in interventions and outcome measures, a meta-analysis was not conducted. Five trials met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 1,503 women, with an average of 301 participants per study. The trials compared the following contraceptive methods: combined oral contraceptive (COC) versus transdermal contraceptive patch, vaginal contraceptive ring, or levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) delivering 20 µg/day; LNG-IUS delivering 12 µg/day versus LNG-IUS delivering 16 µg/day; and LNG-IUS 20 µg/day versus the copper T380A intrauterine device (IUD). In trials comparing two different methods, no significant differences were observed in contraceptive efficacy or continuation rates. However, two of the studies had small sample sizes. The only statistically significant finding was that women in the COC group were more likely to discontinue use for other personal reasons compared to those using the LNG-IUS 20 µg/day (OR 0.27, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.85). However, this finding may have limited clinical relevance. The trial comparing LNG-IUS 12 µg/day and LNG-IUS 16 µg/day demonstrated similar efficacy over one and three years. In three trials evaluating different LNG-IUS devices, continuation rates were at least 75% over periods ranging from 6 to 36 months. The authors concluded that the overall quality of evidence was moderate to low, primarily due to limitations in trial design or incomplete reporting. Different doses of LNG-IUS did not appear to affect efficacy over three years. In one study, continuation rates for LNG-IUS were at least as high as those for COC. However, the current evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the comparative efficacy and continuation rates of hormonal and intrauterine contraceptive methods in women aged 25 years and younger.
